source.text: Xuanzang, trans., Sutra of the Merit of the Original Vows of the Medicine Master of Lapis Light (Taishō T450): selections from the introduction, the twelve great vows and the Pure Lapis world. The closing mantra is the dhāraṇī from Yijing, trans., Sutra of the Seven Medicine Buddhas (T451)

ys01.heading: The Setting of the Assembly
ys01.plain: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha, traveling through many lands teaching, came to the city of Vaiśālī and stayed beneath a tree of sweet sounds. With him were eight thousand great monks and thirty-six thousand bodhisattvas, kings, ministers, brahmins and householders, gods, dragons, yakṣas and countless others, seated around him in reverence, and the Buddha taught the Dharma for them.
ys01.commentary: This introduces where the Medicine Buddha Sutra was taught. Vaiśālī is rendered in Chinese as "the city of vast adornment." Monastics and lay people, humans and non-humans all gathered, showing that this teaching is for all beings.

ys02.heading: Mañjuśrī's Request
ys02.plain: Then Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha's power, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, bowed and joined his palms, and said: "World-Honored One, please tell us the names of such Buddhas and the surpassing merit of the great vows they originally made, so that the karmic obstacles of those who hear may vanish, and to benefit and gladden the beings of the age of the semblance Dharma."
ys02.commentary: Mañjuśrī, bodhisattva of wisdom, requests the teaching for beings of later times. The age of the semblance Dharma is a time when the Buddha is gone and only the outward form of the teaching continues; the Medicine Buddha's vows become a refuge in just such a time.

ys03.heading: The Medicine Buddha of the Eastern Pure Lapis World
ys03.plain: The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: "East of here, beyond Buddha-lands ten times as many as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world called Pure Lapis. Its Buddha is Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaiḍūryaprabha Tathāgata, the Medicine Master of Lapis Light, complete with all ten titles of a Tathāgata. Mañjuśrī, when the Medicine Master of Lapis Light Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made twelve great vows so that all beings would obtain whatever they seek."
ys03.commentary: As Amitābha dwells in the Western Land of Bliss, the Medicine Buddha dwells in the eastern Pure Lapis world. "Medicine Master" means physician, and "Lapis Light" means shining like clear lapis: he is the Buddha who heals the illnesses of body and mind. The twelve vows that follow are the heart of this sutra.

ys04.heading: First Great Vow · A Radiant Body
ys04.plain: The first great vow: When I attain supreme awakening in a future life, may the light of my body blaze forth and shine on measureless worlds, may my body be adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty fine features, and may all beings become just like me.
ys04.commentary: From the very first vow, he wishes not that he alone shine, but that all beings become like him. The Mahāyāna heart of sharing awakening rather than enjoying it alone runs through all twelve vows.

ys05.heading: Second Great Vow · Light in the Darkness
ys05.plain: The second great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may my body be like lapis, clear inside and out and spotlessly pure, its light vast and its merit towering, my body adorned with a net of light brighter than sun and moon, so that beings in darkness all awaken, go where they intend, and accomplish what they wish to do.
ys05.commentary: The "Lapis Light" in the Medicine Buddha's name comes from this vow. Darkness can also mean ignorance and helplessness. It is a vow to be light for those who cannot see the way, so they can walk it themselves.

ys06.heading: Third Great Vow · A Life Lacking Nothing
ys06.plain: The third great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, with boundless wisdom and skillful means may I let all beings obtain inexhaustibly whatever they need to use and enjoy, so that no being lacks anything.
ys06.commentary: The Medicine Buddha's vows attend not only to awakening of the mind but to eating, dressing and living. It is a compassion that does not ignore reality: practice is possible only when life's basics are met.

ys07.heading: Fourth Great Vow · Onto the Right Path
ys07.plain: The fourth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may all beings on wrong paths rest securely on the path of awakening, and may all who follow the paths of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, seeking only their own liberation, stand on the path of the Great Vehicle.
ys07.commentary: A vow to lead beings from wrong paths to the right one, and from practice for oneself to practice for all. It does not belittle śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it means helping them move toward a broader heart.

ys08.heading: Fifth Great Vow · Keeping the Precepts
ys08.plain: The fifth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may the countless beings who practice purely within my teaching all keep the precepts without fail and be complete in the three pure precepts; and if any should break the precepts, on hearing my name may they become pure again and not fall into evil paths.
ys08.commentary: He does not abandon those who stumble while trying to keep the precepts. It is a vow that gives hope: even after doing wrong, one can rise again and become pure.

ys09.heading: Sixth Great Vow · A Whole Body
ys09.plain: The sixth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may beings whose bodies are weak and whose senses are impaired, who cannot see, hear or speak, whose limbs or backs are bent, who suffer from skin diseases, mental illness and every kind of sickness, on hearing my name all become upright and wise, whole in body and free of all illness.
ys09.commentary: It names and attends, one by one, to the pain of those whose bodies are impaired or ill. It is a vow worthy of the Buddha who is a physician: never to turn away from the sick.

ys10.heading: Seventh Great Vow · Ending Illness, Bringing Ease
ys10.plain: The seventh great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may beings tormented by many illnesses, with no one to save them and nowhere to turn, without doctor or medicine, without family or home, living in poverty and suffering, if my name passes through their ears even once, be freed of all illness, at peace in body and mind, with family and livelihood in abundance, and finally attain supreme awakening.
ys10.commentary: This vow is at the center of devotion to the Medicine Buddha. He first thinks of the most helpless person, struck at once by illness, poverty and loneliness, and vows to bring them healing of the body, abundance in life, and even awakening.

ys11.heading: Eighth Great Vow · Freedom from Women's Suffering
ys11.plain: The eighth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may any woman who is tormented by the many sufferings women endure, deeply weary and wishing to leave that body behind, on hearing my name be transformed into a man's body with a man's features, and finally attain supreme awakening.
ys11.commentary: In the ancient India where this sutra arose, women bore heavy suffering, from the pain of childbirth to social discrimination. This vow answered the wish to escape that suffering in such a reality. Today it is usually understood not as saying a woman's body is lower, but as compassion that seeks to free people from discrimination and suffering. Elsewhere Mahāyāna sutras also teach that male and female forms are themselves empty.

ys12.heading: Ninth Great Vow · To Right View
ys12.plain: The ninth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may I free beings from the net of Māra and release them from the bonds of wrong teachings, lead those lost in the dense forest of wrong views to rest in right view, and let them gradually cultivate the bodhisattva practices and swiftly attain supreme awakening.
ys12.commentary: An illness of thought is as fearsome as an illness of the body. Wrong views are like a dense forest, hard to get out of. It is a vow to take people by the hand and lead them out of that forest onto the right path.

ys13.heading: Tenth Great Vow · For the Imprisoned and Oppressed
ys13.plain: The tenth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may beings caught by the laws of the land, bound, beaten, imprisoned or sentenced to punishment, or who suffer countless other disasters and humiliations, crushed by grief and worry and pained in body and mind, on hearing my name be freed from all sorrow and suffering by the power of my merit and might.
ys13.commentary: It attends even to the suffering of the imprisoned, oppressed and humiliated. It carries the comfort that no one, whatever their situation, is abandoned.

ys14.heading: Eleventh Great Vow · Food for the Hungry
ys14.plain: The eleventh great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may beings tormented by hunger and thirst, who even do harm in seeking food, on hearing my name and holding it single-mindedly, first be filled with fine food, and afterward be brought at last to peace by the taste of the Dharma.
ys14.commentary: The order is striking: first fill them with food, then with the taste of the Dharma. One does not preach first to the hungry. It shows that caring for the body is where compassion begins.

ys15.heading: Twelfth Great Vow · Clothing for the Destitute
ys15.plain: The twelfth great vow: When I attain awakening in a future life, may beings so poor they have no clothes, tormented day and night by mosquitoes and gadflies, cold and heat, on hearing my name and holding it single-mindedly, obtain fine clothes as they wish, and jeweled ornaments, garlands and incense, music and entertainment, enjoying all to their heart's content.
ys15.commentary: The last vow promises clothing, beauty and even enjoyment. The twelve vows end with a generous heart that wants beings to enjoy the very pleasures of living.

ys16.heading: The Pure Lapis World
ys16.plain: Mañjuśrī, these are the twelve wondrous and lofty vows that the Medicine Master of Lapis Light Tathāgata made while practicing the bodhisattva path. That Buddha's land is pure throughout, with no evil paths and no sounds of suffering. Its ground is lapis, its roads marked by golden cords, and its city walls, palaces, pavilions, windows and nets are all made of the seven treasures, no different in merit and adornment from the Western Land of Bliss. In that land dwell two bodhisattvas, Sunlight Universally Shining and Moonlight Universally Shining, foremost among the countless bodhisattvas.
ys16.commentary: The Medicine Buddha is attended by Sunlight Bodhisattva and Moonlight Bodhisattva. They are the two bodhisattvas enshrined on either side of the Medicine Buddha in temple Medicine Buddha halls, meaning that beings are lit day and night alike.

ys17.heading: Mantra of the Medicine Buddha
ys17.meaning: I take refuge in the Medicine Master Lapis Light King Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One. Thus it is: oṃ, medicine, medicine, arisen from medicine, svāhā.
ys17.commentary: Also called the Medicine Buddha's Consecration Mantra. It is not in Xuanzang's translation but comes from Yijing's Sutra of the Seven Medicine Buddhas, and is widely chanted in Medicine Buddha prayer in Korea.
ys17.plain: A mantra that takes refuge in the Medicine Buddha and asks for healing. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

manjusri.definition: The bodhisattva who embodies wisdom. "Prince of the Dharma" is an honorific meaning the son who will succeed the Buddha, the Dharma King.

xiangfa.definition: The second of the three ages after the Buddha's passing (true Dharma, semblance Dharma, final Dharma): the form of teaching and practice remains, but few awaken.

bhaisajyaguru.definition: Bhaiṣajyaguru, Buddha of the eastern Pure Lapis world: the "physician Buddha" who heals beings' illnesses of body and mind, shown holding a medicine bowl.

vaidurya.definition: A clear, bluish gem (taken to be lapis lazuli or beryl), not the glass of today. It symbolizes the spotless light of awakening.

ganga-sand.definition: The sands of the Ganges River: an image for numbers beyond counting.

anuttara-bodhi.definition: Supreme, right and complete awakening: the awakening of a Buddha.

sravaka.definition: Śrāvakas awaken by hearing the Buddha's teaching; pratyekabuddhas awaken alone to the principle of conditions without a teacher. Mahāyāna sees these as paths that stop at one's own liberation.

three-pure-precepts.definition: The three precepts of a bodhisattva: refraining from harm, doing good, and benefiting beings.

sun-moon-bodhisattvas.definition: The two bodhisattvas who attend the Medicine Buddha on either side, lighting beings day and night like the sun and moon.

mantra.definition: The true words of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, chanted in their original sound rather than translated. Long ones are called dhāraṇī.
